one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with thanks to Tony Tan Caktiong (Apec 2015 CEO Summit conference chair and Jollibee board chair, 9th largest QSR globally by market cap) for the 'ringside seat' on the first row to hear Obama on climate change, Xi Jinping on trade pacts, Medvedev on terrorism, and several other leaders. But by far, in his humble opinion, Alibaba executive chair Jack Ma delivered the most moving speech: the 51-year-old self-made Chinese billionaire and former school teacher (Forbes-rated $23.3 billion, richest in China, 18th in the world) explained with passion and conviction that the Internet is the economic equalizer in our globalized world. Online, impoverished but ingenious manufacturers can reach any buyer in the world -- Laguna wood carvers and embroiderers, Manila tailors selling to New York, London, Beijing -- something nearly impossible in 1989 when Apec was born. Alibaba facilitates delivery and payment via Alipay digital money at the cheapest rates; by 2020 it will account for $650 billion in Chinese trade. Yet Alibaba 'does not own any factory. It is merely an enabler.' In only 15 years it became the biggest Chinese Internet marketplace, founded in a small shack by Ma and 16 friends, half (including Ma) not knowing how to operate a PC. It outsells the older Amazon, largest US online trader, and almost equals Walmart's revenue. Rocket International was formed in Germany two years ago to dominate Internet trading outside the US and China. Apec and WTO both aim to support sustainable economic growth and prosperity by championing free and open trade -- believing in competition through drastically lowering tariffs, quotas, and taxes; privatizing public assets and utilities; deregulating prices and businesses. Unlike WTO, however, Apec is mostly a forum without binding character; the WTO, EU, and Asean require compliance. Upholding membership in both Apec and WTO, Philippine presidents -- especially FVR -- robustly promoted free trade and implemented globalization, deregulation, privatization, and liberalization: telecom, banking, insurance, and airline industries liberated from monopoly; water utilities and tollways privatized; oil business and power generation deregulated. Economist-friend Romeo L. Bernardo's data: GDP growth from 2.9% annual average (1991-2000, first decade of globalization) to 4.8% (2001-2010) to about 5.9% (2011-2014); inflation reduced from 8.3% (1996) to 1.4% present. Critics lament these statistics benefit mostly the rich while the poor wallow in low pay, malnutrition, inadequate shelter, ill health -- they vehemently oppose Apec/WTO globalization. CJ notes the rich-first trajectory is equally evident in the US's 20th-century industrial rise and China's 21st-century digital rise. To hasten the propoor trajectory, Apec leaders now stress inclusive growth -- the call to assist MSMEs (micro, small, medium enterprises) is as loud as advocacies for liberalization and deregulation, hence the concurrent MSME summit. President Obama's 'unorthodox moderating' of a panel composed of Jack Ma and Aisa Mijeno -- the young Filipina who pioneered electricity from salt water -- drew the most applause, showing entrepreneurial ingenuity at its best, an accomplished giant and a very promising startup both buoyed by free enterprise. Ma's rags-to-riches story shows how entrepreneurship and innovation can bridge the gap between poor inventors/producers and unreachable foreign markets, while providing the needed financial, marketing, and logistics muscles. Indeed, the Internet is the globalization equalizer that worked for Ma. It should equally work for Mijeno.
